name.text: Retaining wall — draw the line of best fit and predict

questiontext.text:
Engineers model the maximum mass of soil \(y\) (tonnes) a retaining wall can hold against its height \(x\) (metres). Data were collected for walls from \(1\) m to \(6\) m tall, plotted below.

1) Drag the two red points to draw a suitable line of best fit through the data.

[[jsxgraph input-ref-ans1="rP1" input-ref-ans2="rP2" width="540px" height="480px"]] var DX=[1,2,3,4,5,6]; var DY=[{#py1#},{#py2#},{#py3#},{#py4#},{#py5#},{#py6#}]; var YMAX={#float(ymaxw)#}; var brd = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox:[-1, YMAX, 8, -3], axis:true, grid:true, keepaspectratio:false, showCopyright:false, showNavigation:false}); brd.create('text',[7.8, -1.4, 'Height x (m)'],{anchorX:'right',fixed:true,fontSize:12,cssStyle:'font-weight:bold;color:#333'}); brd.create('text',[0.15, YMAX-0.6, 'Soil mass y (t)'],{anchorX:'left',fixed:true,fontSize:12,cssStyle:'font-weight:bold;color:#333'}); for (var i=0;i<6;i++){ brd.create('point',[DX[i],DY[i]],{name:'',fixed:true,color:'#000000',fillColor:'#000000',size:3}); } var P1 = brd.create('point',[1,1],{name:'',color:'#cc0000',fillColor:'#cc0000',size:5,snapToGrid:true,snapSizeX:0.5,snapSizeY:0.5}); var P2 = brd.create('point',[6,7],{name:'',color:'#cc0000',fillColor:'#cc0000',size:5,snapToGrid:true,snapSizeX:0.5,snapSizeY:0.5}); brd.create('line',[P1,P2],{strokeColor:'#cc0000',strokeWidth:2,straightFirst:true,straightLast:true}); stack_jxg.bind_point(rP1, P1); stack_jxg.bind_point(rP2, P2); [[/jsxgraph]]
[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]
[[feedback:prtSlope]] [[feedback:prtInt]]

2) Use your line to predict the soil mass for a \({@xp@}\) m tall mega-structure wall.

\( y \approx \) [[input:ansPred]] [[validation:ansPred]] \(\ \mathrm{t}\) [[feedback:prtPred]]

3) How reliable is this prediction?

[[input:ansRel]] [[validation:ansRel]] [[feedback:prtRel]]

generalfeedback.text:
1) A good line of best fit for this data has the equation \[ y = {@m*x+c@}. \] (slope \(m={@m@}\) tonnes per metre, \(y\)-intercept \(c={@c@}\)). The correct line is shown in blue below.

2) Substituting \(x={@xp@}\): \[ y = {@m@}\times{@xp@} + ({@c@}) = {@yp@}\ \mathrm{t}. \]

3) The data only covers \(1\) m to \(6\) m. Predicting at \({@xp@}\) m is well outside this range — an extrapolation — so the prediction is less reliable: the linear relationship may not continue for such tall walls.

[[jsxgraph width="480px" height="440px"]] var DX=[1,2,3,4,5,6]; var DY=[{#py1#},{#py2#},{#py3#},{#py4#},{#py5#},{#py6#}]; var M={#float(m)#}, C={#float(c)#}, YMAX={#float(ymaxw)#}; var brd = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox:[-1, YMAX, 8, -3], axis:true, grid:true, keepaspectratio:false, showCopyright:false, showNavigation:false}); brd.create('text',[7.8, -1.4, 'Height x (m)'],{anchorX:'right',fixed:true,fontSize:12,cssStyle:'font-weight:bold;color:#333'}); brd.create('text',[0.15, YMAX-0.6, 'Soil mass y (t)'],{anchorX:'left',fixed:true,fontSize:12,cssStyle:'font-weight:bold;color:#333'}); brd.create('functiongraph',[function(x){ return M*x + C; }, 0, 7.5],{strokeColor:'#1f4fd8', strokeWidth:2, highlight:false}); for (var i=0;i<6;i++){ brd.create('point',[DX[i],DY[i]],{name:'',fixed:true,color:'#000000',fillColor:'#000000',size:3}); } [[/jsxgraph]]

falsefeedback.text: Check where your line meets the \(y\)-axis (its intercept) — it should sit near \(y={@c@}\).
Substitute \(x={@xp@}\) into the equation of your line: \(y=mx+c\).
The prediction is far outside the data range (1 m to 6 m). Predicting beyond the data is extrapolation, which is less reliable.
The gradient of your line is too far from the trend of the points. Aim for a line that rises about \({@m@}\) tonnes for every extra metre.

Line wrong (shallow); prediction wrong; reliability wrong
